issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal of feared uncontrollable rage is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no corresponding trigger, threat, memory, or strategy items suggesting anger-driven reactivity, aggression risk, or conflict; the other appraisals instead center on shame and hopelessness after rape. This makes the rage item clinically discordant within the selected five components.

issues.item: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
issues.explanation: The strategy of constant socialising is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile in this rape-related presentation. The selected triggers are solitary/sensory reminders (silence, outdoor smells, anniversary), and the appraisals are shame, suicidality, and feared rage. Constantly surrounding oneself with people does not connect clearly to these reminders and is somewhat at odds with body shame after rape, making it the least coherent avoidance/coping item here.

vignette: Forty years ago, during an early autumn harvest, Amara Jenkins was working past the eastern treeline when the shadow detached itself from the soybean rows. The violation lasted hours, but what etched itself into her nervous system was the sudden, suffocating silence that followed—no crickets, no wind, just the flat quiet of a landscape holding its breath—and the thick, loamy scent of overturned earth clinging to her skin. When she finally dragged herself home, the soil smell followed her into every room, a permanent marker of what had been done to her in the dark. As the years passed, that single September night colonized her present. Every October, when the calendar turned to the anniversary, the air would grow heavy, and the mere whisper of dirt under her boots would pull her back to the field. She began to equate the ground itself with violation; the rich black soil that fed her livelihood now smelled of loss. In her mind, the contamination seeped inward. She could scrub until her knuckles cracked, but the feeling of being permanently soiled never left. That sense of defilement warred with a deeper conviction: that a body used so roughly, stained so thoroughly, could never hold value again. She started questioning whether any of the years she had gathered were enough to justify continuing. To survive the weight of those thoughts, Amara built walls of silence and repetition. When the yardage sounds outside the barn suddenly died down, forcing her back toward the field, she immediately retreated to the house and refused any physical contact from her husband. The sensory trigger demanded escape, but the sudden silence alone was enough to convince her that the contamination seeped inward, reinforcing the conviction that she could never truly be clean. Believing herself fundamentally defiled, she forced herself to catalog every small blessing in the day, counting harvest bonuses and garden yields until her mind stopped spiraling. The positive reframing was meant to be a shield, but the mental effort only reminded her how corrupted she felt, which in turn made the scent of fresh tilled earth impossible to ignore. Avoidance of the dusk light kept the dark at bay, yet by refusing to engage with it, she taught her nervous system that silence was a threat worth bracing for. Each strategy she deployed to feel safe only sharpened the memory of the soil and solidified the belief that her life had lost its anchor, turning every quiet evening into a waiting room for shame. The avoidance became a quiet erosion of her days. She stopped walking the property line with her partner, claiming her knees could no longer handle the uneven ground, which left him reaching out across the breakfast table to no avail. Her work in the crops narrowed to sunlit mornings, and she hired a seasonal hand to manage the evening irrigation, paying a premium just to keep her boots from touching the dew-heavy rows after sundown. The isolation compounded over decades. By the time she reached seventy-four, the positive thoughts no longer stuck, the avoidance left her utterly alone, and the shame felt too heavy to carry into winter. She has come to seek counseling not because she wants to relive the field, but because she fears the relationship will fracture completely without intervention. She hopes, despite her certainty, that someone might help her untangle the knot without forcing her back into the dirt.
